claims.text: The initial single-crystal FeNiCrMn alloy is in a metastable FCC state.
The initial alloy is free of pre-existing BCC precipitates.
FeNiCrMn has high lattice distortion caused by atomic-size mismatch.
The anomalous strain-rate insensitivity of yield strength is driven by thermally activated partial-dislocation nucleation at lattice-distortion sites.
FCC-to-BCC transformation is not the mechanism driving the onset of yielding.
FCC-to-BCC transformation at yielding is kinetically inhibited by high stacking-fault-energy barriers.
At cryogenic temperatures, low stacking-fault energy and lattice distortion stabilize partial dislocations and stacking faults.
Lattice distortion limits partial-dislocation mobility.
Restricted dislocation mobility suppresses activation of phase-transformation pathways at the yield point.
Thermal fluctuations lower the activation barrier for partial-dislocation nucleation.
The partial-dislocation nucleation barrier remains high enough to prevent significant strain-rate sensitivity.
The critical stress for BCC-phase nucleation exceeds the yield stress.
FCC-to-BCC transformation requires higher strain or different thermodynamic conditions, such as high pressure or particular temperature ranges.
Yield strength will vary minimally with strain rate from 10^-4 to 10^3 s^-1 throughout 77–600 K.
Partial-dislocation nucleation and stacking-fault formation will dominate deformation at yielding.
No detectable BCC phase will form at the yield point.
FCC-to-BCC transformation will occur only at significantly higher strain or under compression or high pressure.
The hypothesis applies to single-crystal FeNiCrMn through 600 K but may not apply to polycrystals or temperatures above 600 K.
Testing both [111] and [100] orientations can reveal crystal-orientation anisotropy.
Observation of FCC-to-BCC transformation at the onset of plasticity, correlated with yield strength, would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes suppression of transformation to high stacking-fault-energy barriers, whereas the structural mediator invokes low stacking-fault energy at cryogenic temperatures. The distinction between an activation barrier and the stacking-fault energy itself is not explained, leaving the energetic premise internally inconsistent or ambiguous.
